summary:
The Penal Code criminalises consensual sexual activity between men and between women. The provisions are inherited from the colonial period and carry a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment. ILGA World Database, the Human Dignity Trust country profile and general reference coverage record the same offence and the same statutory maximum.

No arrests or prosecutions appear in the record. United States State Department human-rights reports for 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 record no arrests or prosecutions directed at LGBT people; the 2011 report records no LGBT-specific abuses; the 2013 report records no abuses by security forces and no prosecutions under the penal-code provisions. The Human Dignity Trust documents no recorded prosecutions in recent years. Reference coverage states the law is not enforced.

Official opposition to any legal change is on the record. Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare publicly opposed same-sex marriage in a 2017 address to a church group. In June 2018 Governor General Sir Frank Kabui used a Queen's Birthday address to warn that same-sex marriage "cannot populate the world", and in the same period acknowledged that being gay or lesbian "is said to be biological and is beyond individual control" while condemning any legal change and citing both the criminal code and the Bible.

No same-sex marriage law exists and Parliament has not legislated one. No form of relationship recognition is available. No non-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity. Reference coverage notes that LGBT people face legal challenges not experienced by other residents.
tangentialFactors:
Reform has been proposed and rejected. In December 2008 the Law Reform Commission proposed legalising sexual activity between people of the same sex; the proposal drew strong opposition and was not adopted. The government told the United Nations in 2011 that it had no intention of decriminalising.

Constitutional reform has narrowed the protection on offer. A 2009 draft constitution listed "sexual orientation" as a prohibited ground of discrimination; the 2011, 2013 and 2014 drafts dropped it. Reform was still under way as of 2019.
localsOnly:
Residents who are trans live under the same Penal Code provisions, which criminalise consensual sexual activity between men and between women and carry a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment. No prosecutions have been recorded in recent years.

No non-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and no form of relationship recognition is available to residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific data is sourced. The material covers sexual orientation and same-sex conduct; nothing in the inventory records the treatment of trans people by police, courts, employers or service providers, and no trans-specific violence or discrimination figures are available.

The enforcement record rests on United States State Department reporting for 2010 to 2013 and on the Human Dignity Trust's assessment of recent years. No more recent prosecution data is sourced, and no domestic figures are available.

No information is sourced on identity-document or gender-marker rules, on entry and visa practice, or on access to facilities and healthcare.

The status of constitutional reform is sourced only to 2019.
